speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Witnessing your child's first words and first steps are magical moments for any parent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I feel lucky to have been there for my three daughters through their years of laughter, tears, tantrums and, of course, joy over unboxing LOL dolls.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Children do grow up so quickly and these precious, fleeting moments will never happen again.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is time we will never get back.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Unfortunately, for most of our low-wage migrant workers, these are milestones they will experience only through phone screens, from thousands of miles away.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: During that trip, I met the wives, parents, siblings and children of Nee Soon Town Council cleaners who had not had the opportunity to visit home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I watched these family members video-call our Nee Soon cleaners in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I could hardly bear the sight as they wept with heartache and longing for one another.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I met so many of our cleaners' families who have never met their fathers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is the same for Hanif's son, Al Ameen, who is now three years old.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hanif has not been there to watch his son grow up.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He proudly shows me all the photos of his son on his phone, including this morning when we met.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But deep inside, I know how painful it must be for him to not be there with his family.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure our migrant workers all wish to be home with their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But they know that working here gives their family a chance at a better life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hanif's wife, Tania, shared quite painfully: "Sometimes, I think, if he can come back to Bangladesh, how amazing that would be.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I feel sad and I miss his presence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, reality is very tough, so he has to work hard abroad for us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Obviously, I feel sad for my son that he will be deprived of his dad's love and affection".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Hanif sums it up, "We are poor people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To survive, we have to make these kinds of sacrifices."  Sir, our migrant workers make extraordinary sacrifices to be here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They deserve to be treated with fairness and dignity like anyone else.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Unfortunately, this has not been the case for many migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, I will outline three major problems they face: kickbacks, confinement and exhaustion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will also propose feasible and impactful solutions to solve these problems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, many workers are forced to pay kickbacks to their employers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This does not even include the unreported cases and could just be the tip of the iceberg.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are workers earning the lowest salaries in Singapore, forced to return their pay cheques to their bosses just so they would not be fired.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For these men, being sent home is to be sentenced to financial ruin.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They would have no way to repay the loans each of them took to make their way here in the first place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These workers were terrified when they spoke to me.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They feared the repercussions of reporting their bosses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What would happen to their job, family and debts?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I could see their hands trembling as they spoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A crime had been committed against them, yet their first emotion was not anger but fear.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One of the workers told me, "When I came to Singapore in 2016, I paid $14,000, then in 2018, I paid $1,500 for my Work Permit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Now they said that if I don’t give them $3,000 they will fire me.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am a really poor man, I have no money to give them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this situation, I am really helpless and feeling depressed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am an honest and hardworking man." Sir, hearing these stories first-hand reminded me that these 960 cases are not just a statistic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are humans with mothers, fathers and families, suffering a grave injustice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But let us, for a moment, talk about numbers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOM says that these cases form "only about 10% of all complaints that MOM receives." This is the wrong comparison.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should be clear about what a forced kickback is.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is employers forcing migrant workers, who have no choice but to pay money.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Forced kickbacks are just as damaging to Singapore's rule of law as corruption cases punishable under the Prevention of Corruption Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For a nation founded and built on the principle of zero tolerance for corruption, forced kickbacks are an equally severe problem that we have not adequately tackled.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, we need to treat kickbacks as seriously as corruption by sharply increasing penalties against employers and individuals caught collecting kickbacks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I agree with Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon when he said that strict penalties and a strong stance against employers who collect kickbacks are key and that deterrence should be on the side of the employers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the current maximum sentence of two years of imprisonment and a $30,000 fine under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act is far too low to be a deterrent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Kickbacks are just as damaging as bribes to the integrity of Singapore's systems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second proposal is to create a permanent scheme that allows migrant workers to change employers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, we have a temporary programme called the Retention Scheme.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This was introduced last year by MOM and the Singapore Contractors Association Limited, or SCAL.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This scheme reduces COVID-19-related labour shortages, but also can allow workers to leave abusive employers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is an age-old solution that all of us already benefit from.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If your boss abuses you and steals from your pay cheque, your first step is surely not to stick around.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is to say I quit and find a new job.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why should migrant workers not get this same opportunity?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My proposal here is not only to make the Retention Scheme a permanent one, but to make it better.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOM said last October that there are plans to cover the manufacturing and marine sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we can do more and cover all sectors that employ Work Permit holders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Workers should not face a decreased salary, employers should not see bidding wars and Singaporeans should not expect price inflation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But there is a second problem that traps workers, literally: physical confinement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In a few weeks' time, we will reach a two-year anniversary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It marks two years since our migrant workers have been free to leave their dormitories.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They leave their dormitories almost exclusively for work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They do get to use recreation centres (RCs), but these are hardly any substitute for the community, with their limited physical amenities and, most importantly, the absence of the workers' social network.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the words of Bangladeshi worker Zakir: "It's like we are inside a cage." He described the mental torture of being allowed out of the dormitory only to go to work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He shared how the continued confinement will lead to mental health issues amongst our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another worker, Sharif, said, "This is prison life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a captive's life." Sir, some feel that RCs are a solution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But as Zakir shares, going to the RC only helps a little.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Like all of us, migrant workers want to meet friends who are living in other areas in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They miss one another, a feeling we all understand.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOM has said that the movement restrictions are "to protect the health of our migrant workers and to mitigate the risk of further transmission".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But, for Sharif, he feels more like he is being punished than being protected.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But these are needs that migrant workers living in dormitories have been denied for far too long now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our lockdown of migrant workers is also not grounded in risk management principles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Migrant workers, by and large, are at very low risk of putting our healthcare system under a strain.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Dormitory residents today have to undergo the Fast and Easy Testing-Rostered Routine.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means they are tested once every seven days.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By contrast, the vast majority of Singaporeans do not undergo routine testing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, their place of residence is audited and enforced with health controls.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All dormitories are configured to implement Safe Living Measures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Large dormitories face Infection Prevention and Control audits at least once a week.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Residents must also complete mandatory COVID-19 education programmes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By contrast, only about 87% of Singapore's overall population is fully vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What more could we ask from our migrant workers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do understand that dormitories are communal places that carry a heightened level of risk.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we do not place residents of military dormitories under nearly the same kind of restrictions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would it be acceptable to bar NSFs from booking out for their entire two years of National Service, in the spirit of protecting them?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why do we treat migrant workers living in dormitories differently?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When in the community, dormitory residents will have to comply with all existing safety measures that the general public already have to comply with, such as mask wearing and dining group sizes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Workers should be required to demonstrate understanding of these measures prior to leaving their dormitories by completing quizzes on the FWMOMCare app.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Those found in breach of these measures should face a graduated scale of penalties, including restricted access to the community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know that Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will share that MOM already has some limited programmes for allowing dormitory residents into the community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Up to 3,000 vaccinated migrant workers may visit the community on weekdays and up to 6,000 on weekends and public holidays.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, they are working with community partners to plan and organise events and activities for workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Surely, we will all agree that this is not nearly enough.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would we all sitting here accept letting only 2% of our NSFs into the community?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This drip-drip offering of tiny community visits does not help the vast majority of workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A broad-based relaxation of movement controls is needed and small-scale community visits are not an adequate substitute.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These measures allow NSFs to remain part of our community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If there are any additional assurances required before our migrant workers can be allowed into the community, can we apply the same measures for NSFs to our migrant workers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The third and final problem I will highlight today is exhaustion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Workers need rest, whether they think they need it or not.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We already accept this by mandating holidays and leave entitlements to workers covered under the Employment Act, and by soon requiring foreign domestic workers to take at least one rest day a month.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But this benefit has not been extended to other migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not just a matter of consistency; it is a matter of safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It should be no wonder to us that burned-out, overworked workers, pushed to their limits, break the rules and get sloppy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To some extent, we can blame errant individuals, but we also have to accept the biological fact that a worker’s body, eventually, hits a limit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Workplace fatigue has been known as a contributing factor of workplace injuries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This aligns with what we will apply to foreign domestic workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we all agree that foreign domestic workers need one mandatory rest day a month, then how can we not agree that migrant workers also need one mandatory rest day a month?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There need to be much harsher penalties against such law-breaking employers and individuals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Workers also need a universal and permanent programme that allows them to switch employers, with salary limits, to ensure labour costs do not spike.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the vast majority of migrant workers living in dormitories remain without access to the community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Small-scale releases should not be seen as the solution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They should be required not to work for that day, similar to foreign domestic workers, so they have some minimum level of rest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This keeps them healthy and would also improve workplace safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are core problems facing too many migrant workers in Singapore, and there are feasible, workable, research-based solutions for each of them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am not asking for any special treatment for our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am only asking that they be treated fairly and equally, like the rest of us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My proposals merely extend to migrant workers protocols we already have in place for dealing with corruption in the corporate sector, with health risks in military dormitories and with exhaustion among foreign domestic workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our words matter, but so do our deeds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Migrant workers are members of our society and builders of our nation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Honestly, I feel bad and it does break my heart that I am not able to be there with her today and to spend time with her on this special day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By the time I get home, probably, she will be asleep.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will do my best to make it up to Ella tomorrow and spend some precious time with her.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a painful feeling to not be there for your children, a feeling that migrant workers who are fathers must feel each and every day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do not think any of us can truly understand what they go through.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The very least that we can do is to ensure that we treat them with the fairness and dignity that everyone in Singapore deserves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Indeed, migrant workers have and will continue to contribute immensely to Singapore’s development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And MOM is committed to ensure that our migrant workers are treated fairly and that their employment rights and well-being are safeguarded during their time here in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: MOM agrees with the Member that the collection of employment kickbacks is a serious offence as it shifts the burden of employment costs from employers to workers and increases the debt burden on the migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Thus, MOM undertakes a multi-pronged approach to detect and deter the collection of employment kickbacks from migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Those who abet the collection of kickbacks will face the same penalties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To the Member’s suggestion to increase the penalties for kickback offences to match the maximum penalty for bribery cases, I would like to highlight that accused persons can be charged on a per-worker basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Substantial fines of $7,000 to $12,000 per charge or short imprisonment terms have been imposed by the Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These sentences have not approached the maximum fine or imprisonment term set out under the EFMA currently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This indicates that the current maximum in terms of fine or imprisonment term for the collection of kickbacks has been sufficient for the Courts to impose sentences that reflect the gravity of offences in all previous cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Besides the strict penalties, MOM also actively enforces against employers, unlicensed agents or employment agencies, who collected kickbacks from migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This has helped MOM to proactively detect cases of employment kickbacks, in addition to complaints that we receive directly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Migrant workers who are pressurised into giving kickbacks should step forward and report the matter to MOM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our FAST Team officers were deployed to dormitories or to reach out to the NGOs, many of whom are very active in the dormitories today, such as the Migrant Workers Centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We share the Member’s view that migrant workers who are treated unfairly should be allowed to change employers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Migrant workers with valid employment claims, including those who have been forced to pay kickbacks, are permitted to transfer to another employer and continue working here in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is an important safeguard for migrant workers who have been unfairly treated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In addition, measures are in place to facilitate the retention of experienced Work Permit holders in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Workers can transfer to a new employer at the end of their contract, without the need for the current employer’s consent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is currently allowed in all business sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Retention Scheme in the construction sector is an additional effort to retain workers whose employment has been terminated and who wish to continue working in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Under the Retention Scheme, the Singapore Contractors Association Limited (SCAL) takes over the upkeep and maintenance of these workers and matches them to another employer in the construction sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Since its implementation in September 2021, about 430 workers have been enrolled in the scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We are in discussions with SCAL on extending the Retention Scheme for a few more months, to support the industry in retaining experienced workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: At the same time, as we had announced in November last year, we are working with the respective trade associations and chambers (TACs) to implement the Retention Scheme in the Marine and Process sectors as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The TACs have been preparing for this implementation and, hopefully, would be ready soon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will provide an update on these in due course.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While these Retention Schemes play a part in ameliorating the manpower challenges faced by the industry today, the fundamental solution is to safely increase the inflow of new workers into Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: MOM has, therefore, been facilitating various industry initiatives to progressively allow more Construction, Marine and Process (CMP) sector workers into Singapore safely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Subject to the public health situation, we will continue these efforts to bring in workers safely to support the needs of the industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Member also suggested salary controls for workers who transfer to a new employer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Salary is one of many factors that workers and employers may consider when negotiating a new employment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We should not introduce rigidity into this process by anchoring on an arbitrary salary point or increment rates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Employers and workers should have the flexibility to negotiate employment terms with consideration of various factors, including the worker’s skills and training, and the prevailing market conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Besides ensuring employment standards, we agree with the Member that all employees, including migrant workers, should have sufficient rest to ensure their well-being and safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These protections apply to all employees, including migrant workers and local employees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Employers are also required to grant all employees, including migrant workers, at least one rest day without pay per week, unless there is a prior written agreement between the employer and the employee to work on the rest day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The employee must also be provided monetary compensation for working on his rest day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As a safeguard, employers cannot compel their employees to work on their rest days, unless under exceptional circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Migrant workers who are forced to do so should approach MOM for assistance and we will investigate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We share the Member’s concern on the importance of workplace safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Fatigue and overworking can affect a worker’s safety at work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is why the Workplace Safety and Health (WSH) Council promotes the protection of workers to prevent fatigue through its Total WSH programme, WSH Council guidelines and platforms, such as the annual National WSH Campaign.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Last year’s National WSH Campaign emphasised Care Time for workers to take care of their safety and health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Simple actions, such as regular exercise, constantly being hydrated and having adequate sleep, can improve one’s physical and mental health and allow workers to be more alert to unsafe acts or conditions at their workplaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Lastly, the Member has asked to allow all vaccinated and boosted migrant workers in dormitories to enter the general community as long as they comply with the current safe management measures and testing regimes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We are very mindful that social and recreation activities are important to the well-being of migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: At the same time, we are also responsible for safeguarding their health and reducing disruption to their lives and work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The good health outcomes of our workers residing in dormitories were achieved through the steadfast support and significant efforts from all our stakeholders – dormitory operators, employers and the workers themselves as well as many of the NGOs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With COVID-19 still circulating in Singapore and the recent Omicron wave, we must not lift these rules in the dormitories too quickly and risk a re-ignition of cases which will unwind all the gains that we have so painstakingly made in the last two years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As dormitories are communal settings where transmissions can occur rapidly, MOM’s strategy is, therefore, to take a careful and calibrated approach to progressively allow more migrant workers to visit the community while actively working to make sure that their well-being is taken care of.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, we have allowed a range of social and recreation activities within the dormitories, subject to group size restrictions and safe management measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Second, migrant workers can now visit any Recreation Centre daily.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We are also working with Recreation Centre operators and community partners, as well as NGOs, to introduce programmes and new offerings to make the Recreation Centre visits much more engaging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While the Member highlighted that full-time NSFs similarly stay and work in a communal setting but can remain part of the community, the key difference here is that NSFs would be able to return to their own homes, separate homes, and be quarantined when necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is unlike the dormitory setting where our dormitory-dwelling migrant workers whose fixed place of residence is in a communal setting, making a potential re-ignition of the cases in the dormitories a health risk for many workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Having said that, I must put on record our grateful thanks to our migrant workers for their patience, cooperation and support during this pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I want to assure our migrant workers that, in line with the progressive adjustment of the Safe Management Measures for our general community, MOM will calibrate measures to allow more workers to visit the community while ensuring that the risk of COVID-19 is contained.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I want to wish his daughter a happy birthday as well.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: One minute, so you could go back a bit earlier.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Do we not feel that there is no deterrence and that maybe it is time to review it, at least to see whether it can serve as a deterrent?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As for the extension of the Retention Scheme, as I have said, we are working with the trade associations because there is an implementation mechanism.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If we can open it to more sectors, obviously, we can consider that.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But you need a receptacle – somebody must want to take the responsibility.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So far, we have been talking to trade associations within the process and the marine sectors, who were prepared to do so.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The time allowed for the proceedings has expired.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I adjourn the House pursuant to the Standing Order.
